edition.deck: A disputed execution plan, rising political tensions and a major personal-data breach lead today's coverage.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises consequential current affairs and groups multiple reports about the same event. Allegations and disputed claims are attributed; legal and practical outcomes that remain unresolved are not presented as settled.

content.headline: Ethiopia and Eritrea trade accusations as fighting threatens wider conflict
content.shortHeadline: Ethiopia and Eritrea trade accusations as fighting escalates
content.standfirst: Ethiopia says Eritrean forces crossed into Tigray and calls the move an invasion; Eritrea says Ethiopia started an unprovoked war. Reported drone strikes have raised fears of a wider regional conflict, but casualties remain unverified.

image.caption: Ethiopian forces took control of Tigray's main city, Mekelle, last week.

sources.originalTitle: Ethiopia and Eritrea accuse each other of starting conflict after troops cross border

segments.body: Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of an “all-out invasion” of its northern Tigray region, saying Eritrean forces advanced as far as 60km into the area. Eritrea rejects the accusation and says it is facing an unprovoked war of aggression from its neighbour.

segments.title: A fragile peace under strain
segments.body:
Drone strikes were reported near Adigrat, where a US-based conflict monitor said Eritrean troops and ammunition were hit. Witnesses described strikes and destroyed lorries, but there are no verified reports of casualties. The BBC says it cannot report from Tigray.

The two neighbours blame each other for breaking the 2022 deal that ended Ethiopia’s civil war. Their relations have worsened over Ethiopia’s ambitions for access to an Eritrean Red Sea port, and diplomatic ties were severed last week.

content.headline: US sanctions the International Criminal Court, drawing warning over rule of law
content.shortHeadline: US sanctions the International Criminal Court
content.standfirst: The Trump administration says the ICC unfairly targets Americans and Israeli officials. The court calls the sanctions an attempt to obstruct justice and urges its member states to help it continue its work.

image.caption: The International Criminal Court in The Hague.

sources.originalTitle: US imposes sanctions on international criminal court
USA indfører sanktioner mod international domstol

segments.body: The United States has imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court, escalating its campaign against the tribunal. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the measures would prohibit transactions with the court and restrict its ability to operate. The US is not an ICC member.

segments.title: A dispute over the court's authority
segments.body:
The ICC said the move was an attempt to obstruct justice and an assault on the rule of law and the international legal order. It urged its 125 member states to ensure the court can continue its work.

The administration has objected to ICC arrest warrants for Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The court also investigated alleged crimes by US soldiers in Afghanistan, though that case has since closed.

perspectives.body: DR reports that the sanctions may reach companies providing services to the court, while a US official said Treasury licences could be issued to protect American interests. The administration has not provided further details.

content.headline: Navi Pillay wins Nobel Peace Prize for work on international law
content.shortHeadline: Navi Pillay wins Nobel Peace Prize
content.standfirst: The South African jurist was honoured for promoting peace and international law. Her record includes work on war crimes and a UN commission’s findings on Gaza, which Israel has strongly rejected.

image.caption: Navi Pillay was told of the award at Nuremberg's Palace of Justice.

sources.originalTitle: Navi Pillay, former UN human rights chief, wins Nobel Peace Prize
ICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international law
Nobelprismodtager: 'Hvis I klapper lidt mere, deler jeg måske med Trump'

segments.body: Navi Pillay, the former UN human rights chief and a judge at the International Court of Justice, has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. The Norwegian Nobel Committee cited her efforts to promote peace and international law, saying her work helped strengthen a global legal order.

segments.title: A career and a contested record
segments.body:
Pillay, 85, began her career defending anti-apartheid activists in South Africa and later served on the UN-backed tribunal for Rwanda. From 2021 to 2025 she chaired a commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory. It concluded that Israel had committed genocidal acts in Gaza; Israel rejected the findings and accused the commission of bias. The Nobel Committee said the award was not a position on whether Israel’s offensive amounted to genocide.

Israel’s Foreign Ministry condemned the award. UN human rights chief Volker Türk and South African President Cyril Ramaphosa welcomed it as recognition of human rights, justice and accountability.

content.headline: US execution by firing squad is set to be livestreamed, Pentagon says
content.shortHeadline: Pentagon says Hasan execution will be livestreamed
content.standfirst: The Pentagon says Nidal Hasan’s execution is scheduled for 3 December at Fort Hood. The unprecedented broadcast plan faces questions about legality, access and the potential harm of showing an execution to the public.

image.caption: US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution would be livestreamed.

sources.originalTitle: Firing squad execution to be livestreamed, Pentagon says
Fort Hood survivor supports gunman's execution by firing squad but questions livestream
Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream execution puts US in dubious company
Pentagon: Henrettelse af mand bag massedrab på militærbase skal livestreames
Execution live stream could cause PTSD in viewers, say psychiatrists

segments.body: The Pentagon says it plans to livestream the execution of former US Army major Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 unarmed soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution by firing squad is scheduled for 3 December at the Texas base.

segments.title: Legal and ethical questions
segments.body:
The plan is not certain to go ahead. Legal expert John Mills told the BBC that Hasan’s appeals are not complete and could delay the execution. Army rules restrict attendance at military executions to specified groups, and officials have not explained whether those rules will change or what protections would prevent children from seeing the stream.

A Fort Hood survivor, Alonzo Lunsford, supports the firing squad but questions an uncensored broadcast, particularly for younger viewers. UK psychiatrists cited by the Guardian warned that watching could distress some people, especially those with pre-existing mental health conditions.

perspectives.body: The Guardian places the plan in the context of public executions elsewhere, noting that Hasan could still appeal through civilian federal courts and that the scheduled date does not mean the execution is certain to proceed.

content.headline: ICE agent shoots man in Bronx as New York officials demand answers
content.shortHeadline: ICE agent shoots man in the Bronx
content.standfirst: Oscar Belgal was taken to hospital after an ICE agent fired into his car as his five-year-old son sat in the back, according to New York officials. The Department of Homeland Security cited Belgal’s criminal history; the circumstances remain under dispute.

sources.originalTitle: ICE agent shoots man in New York City

segments.body:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent shot 28-year-old Oscar Belgal in his car in the Bronx, New York, while Belgal’s five-year-old son was in the back seat. Officials said Belgal was alive and in hospital.

The Department of Homeland Security said the officer fired while attempting to arrest a man it described as a “criminal illegal alien”. The department also cited prior convictions and arrests and alleged links to the Trinitarios gang.

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani called the shooting “unconscionable” and said the officer fired multiple rounds into a car with a child inside. Governor Kathy Hochul said she asked President Donald Trump for the release of any body-camera footage. Trump had not publicly commented at the time of the report.

Mamdani said he would ask Trump to end ICE enforcement actions in the city. The BBC has contacted DHS for comment on the mayor’s account.

content.headline: Russian strikes and winter fears push some Kyiv residents to leave
content.shortHeadline: Russian strikes push some Kyiv residents to leave
content.standfirst: Renewed attacks on energy infrastructure and memories of last winter’s power cuts are prompting some families to leave Kyiv. Many residents have not decided whether to go, while the city is preparing backup power and accommodation for vulnerable people.

image.caption: Olena Konoplia explains what she needs to avoid to feel safe outside Kyiv.

sources.originalTitle: Russian strikes and approaching winter force some in Kyiv to pack bags and flee

segments.body: Some Kyiv residents are preparing to leave before winter after renewed Russian attacks on the city and the country’s energy infrastructure. Mariia Shostak is taking her two young children to Egypt, saying she does not feel safe after weeks of attacks and a difficult winter of power cuts and sub-zero temperatures.

segments.title: Choices shaped by attacks and hardship
segments.body:
A September Gradus survey found that 40% of Ukrainians would consider relocating if living conditions continued to deteriorate; 35% said they would not move and 25% were undecided. Another mother told the BBC that missile attacks damaged her home and worsened her young daughter’s anxiety. Others are moving to rural areas within Ukraine.

The city is offering some vulnerable residents places in converted facilities and has built a network of small power plants in fortified locations. The reporting does not suggest a mass departure: many people are weighing safety against work, schooling and the cost of leaving.

content.headline: Anti-migrant protests turn violent in South Africa, police say
content.shortHeadline: Anti-migrant protests turn violent in South Africa
content.standfirst: At least 24 vehicles were set alight and foreign-owned shops were looted in Soweto and Durban, police say. The unrest follows a court ruling on asylum applications, amid anger and false claims about what the ruling means.

image.caption: Police fired rubber bullets to disperse crowds in Durban.

sources.originalTitle: Cars torched and shops looted as anti-migrant violence erupts in South Africa

segments.body: Police say at least 24 vehicles were set alight during anti-immigration protests in Soweto and Durban. Foreign-owned shops were also looted, and gunshots were reported in Soweto. No injuries had been reported in Durban at the time of the report; police deployed reinforcements and said they would pursue those responsible.

segments.title: A ruling and rising tensions
segments.body:
The protests followed a Constitutional Court ruling that people who entered South Africa without documents, or missed immigration deadlines, must be allowed to apply for asylum. The ruling does not automatically grant refugee status or a permanent right to stay; applications are assessed individually.

South Africa’s Home Affairs Department said it would change how it complies with the ruling after staff were overwhelmed and threats to public order emerged. The country has seen repeated xenophobic violence, including attacks in 2008 that killed more than 60 people. Researchers say broad claims that migrants take jobs or drive crime are not supported by evidence.

content.headline: France offers 3,000 supply teachers as student protests continue
content.shortHeadline: France offers 3,000 teachers amid student protests
content.standfirst: The government’s first material concession follows weeks of demonstrations over staffing and resources in secondary schools. Student leaders say they want more concrete action, while violence and closures have accompanied protests in some areas.

image.caption: Thousands gathered at the Bastille during the student protests in Paris.

sources.originalTitle: France promises 3,000 extra teachers in first step to calm student protests

segments.body: France has offered 3,000 supply teachers for around 500 secondary schools identified as most in need, the first material concession since student protests began. Education minister Édouard Geffray said new ministry software would help direct staff to schools with the greatest shortages.

segments.title: A guarded response
segments.body:
The government said 71,000 people protested across France on Thursday. Police used tear gas after some groups attacked them; a school was ransacked in Bordeaux and a deputy head was beaten in Marseille. On Friday, about 140 of France’s 3,500 secondary schools were fully or partly closed, down from earlier days. Another day of action has been called for Tuesday.

Student representatives said they would wait to see whether the promise brings results. One union called for €10bn in investment, while the government has offered no comparable new funding commitment. Officials are also concerned about the country’s debt situation.

content.headline: Labour holds Holborn and St Pancras as Greens face pressure over policy
content.shortHeadline: Labour holds Holborn as Greens face leadership questions
content.standfirst: Sagal Abdi-Wali won 45% of the vote to Green leader Zack Polanski’s 33%, in a low-turnout contest. The result comes amid criticism of the Greens’ policy on Zionism and disputes over Polanski’s absence from the conference vote.

image.caption: Sagal Abdi-Wali, Labour's new MP for Holborn and St Pancras.

sources.originalTitle: Labour fends off Green party to win Holborn and St Pancras byelection
Holborn and St Pancras byelection loss will disappoint Greens – but there may also be relief
‘Zack should go’: How hard-left revolt and antisemitism row turned Greens ‘toxic’
Polanski’s leadership is in crisis. The divided Greens face an uncertain future
Polanski must resign after by-election loss, says leader of Jewish Greens
Leader of Jewish Greens calls for Zack Polanski to resign after byelection loss

segments.body: Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali has won the Holborn and St Pancras byelection with 12,292 votes, 45% of the total. Green leader Zack Polanski finished second with 8,928 votes, or 33%. Turnout was 38.7%, the lowest for an English byelection in this parliament.

segments.title: Pressure within the Greens
segments.body:
The result followed a divisive Green conference vote on a motion equating Zionism with racism and calling for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state. Polanski was campaigning in the constituency rather than attending the debate and vote. He later said he would have opposed the motion as passed; four of the party’s five MPs opposed it.

Former Green leader Caroline Lucas said Polanski should have been present and shown leadership. Vivien Lichtenstein, chair of the Jewish Greens, called for him to resign. Other party members dispute Lichtenstein’s claim to speak for the group, and a no-confidence motion against her was being tabled.

segments.title: What the result may signal
segments.body: Polanski said he could continue as leader and described the Greens’ vote share as a strong byelection performance. The Guardian’s analysis says the result may leave the party competitive in similar seats, while noting that the low turnout and the combined 2024 Green and independent vote raise questions about whether it expanded its support.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s analysis argues that Labour’s win is not necessarily a strong endorsement: the low turnout and modest majority may partly reflect expectations that Labour would hold the seat.

content.headline: King Charles reportedly covers Andrew's £1.5m Royal Lodge bill
content.shortHeadline: King reportedly pays Andrew's £1.5m Royal Lodge bill
content.standfirst: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor owed £1.8m for repairs but received about £302,000 for giving up his lease early, leaving a net payment of £1.5m. Reports say the King used private funds to cover it; the brothers’ repayment arrangements are not public.

image.caption: Royal Lodge, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's former home in Windsor.

sources.originalTitle: King pays Andrew's £1.5m repair bill on Royal Lodge
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor faced £1.8m repair bill after leaving Royal Lodge
King pays Andrew’s £1.5m bill… even as disgraced ex-prince gets £302,000 payoff
Andrew wins legal claim against police over search of his homes

segments.body: The Crown Estate says it received £1.5m after Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor left Royal Lodge. The former prince faced £1.8m in repair and restoration costs but was due about £302,000 in compensation for surrendering the lease early. The Crown Estate said it had paid him no money at the end of the lease.

segments.title: Questions over the arrangement
segments.body:
The BBC and the i Paper report that King Charles used his private funds to cover the net bill, with the i Paper describing the money as a loan. It is not known whether or how Andrew will repay him. The Crown Estate said the property would be marketed for future use and that its focus was generating value for the nation.

The payment comes amid scrutiny of Andrew’s Royal Lodge lease and an earlier National Audit Office report that he had sublet cottages on the estate. He has denied wrongdoing in relation to Jeffrey Epstein.

segments.title: A separate legal challenge
segments.body: Separately, Thames Valley Police accepted that warrants used to search Andrew’s homes were unlawful because they were obtained under the wrong statutory provision. The court ruling did not end the investigation. Police say legal proceedings remain under way over whether they can retain material seized during the searches.

perspectives.body: The i Paper explains that the ruling concerns the legal basis for the searches; it does not determine whether material seized can be used in the ongoing investigation.

content.headline: Government review warns of rising risk of ADHD overdiagnosis
content.shortHeadline: Review warns ADHD diagnoses could lead to overdiagnosis
content.standfirst: Diagnoses among young people have risen sharply, bringing rates close to or above estimated prevalence for some groups. The government-commissioned report says this does not prove widespread overdiagnosis is happening now, but warns the risks are increasing.

image.caption: Rates of ADHD and autism diagnoses have risen over the past decade.

sources.originalTitle: The four reasons why ADHD experts fear the UK is heading towards overdiagnosis

segments.body:
A government-commissioned review says rising rates of ADHD and autism diagnoses mean the risk of overdiagnosis and misdiagnosis is becoming more important. Among teenage boys, the ADHD diagnosis rate rose from 2% to 5% over a decade; among girls, it increased from 0.5% to 2.5%.

The report says the latest research does not establish that overdiagnosis is currently happening at scale. It does find NHS diagnosis rates are approaching, and for some groups exceeding, estimates of how common the conditions are.

segments.title: Why rates are rising
segments.body:
The report discusses several possible drivers: broader definitions, increased awareness, subjective assessment methods, incentives linked to support and benefits, and private clinics. It also notes that waiting lists are lengthening, with some families waiting more than two years. One report author called the findings a warning sign, not a definitive conclusion.

Experts quoted in the report differ on the role of changing understanding and diagnosis. It also recognises that some people remain undiagnosed and that anxiety or other conditions may be mistaken for ADHD.

content.headline: BBC cuts risk losing experienced staff as more than 2,000 jobs go
content.shortHeadline: BBC faces staff exodus as more than 2,000 jobs go
content.standfirst: The corporation is seeking £500m in savings as licence-fee cancellations accelerate. Staff quoted by the i Paper say voluntary redundancies risk taking experienced employees elsewhere, while BBC managers say the changes are difficult but needed.

image.caption: More than 2,000 BBC television and radio jobs are set to go.

sources.originalTitle: BBC faces losing its best talent from news and sport as a result of savage cuts

segments.body: More than 2,000 BBC television and radio jobs are set to go as the corporation seeks £500m in savings. Staff quoted by the i Paper say morale is low and fear voluntary redundancy will encourage experienced employees to leave for other employers.

segments.title: Programming and leadership changes
segments.body:
The BBC has announced cuts to several Radio 4 programmes, including You and Yours, Thinking Allowed and Free Thinking. The report says BBC Three and BBC Scotland broadcast channels may also close, with some content moving online. The BBC says savings are necessary while it invests for the future.

Director-general Matt Brittin outlined plans to change iPlayer and develop an AI assistant, but staff quoted in the report questioned whether the vision could ease concerns over job losses and funding. The BBC disputes the suggestion that low morale applies across the organisation.

content.headline: Cop31 host urges richer nations to spend more on climate security
content.shortHeadline: Cop31 host calls for much greater climate spending
content.standfirst: Turkey’s climate minister says wealthy countries should spend far more on climate than the 5% of GDP promised for defence. Pacific leaders at a pre-summit meeting also pressed for accessible climate finance and urgent action to keep warming within 1.5C.

image.caption: Turkey's climate minister Murat Kurum meets Australia's prime minister Anthony Albanese at the pre-Cop31 summit in Fiji.

sources.originalTitle: Cop31 host urges wealthy countries to spend ‘much more’ on climate than defence

segments.body: Murat Kurum, Turkey’s climate minister and president-designate of Cop31, said wealthy countries should spend “much more” on climate than the 5% of GDP Nato members have pledged for defence. “The climate issue is the security issue itself,” he said at a pre-summit meeting in Fiji.

segments.title: Pacific priorities and a disputed transition
segments.body:
Pacific leaders called for climate finance to reach vulnerable communities and for efforts to keep the 1.5C warming limit within reach. Australia’s climate minister said only 0.2% of global climate finance was spent helping small island states adapt. A UN environment report cited at the meeting said even the most optimistic pathway would lead to at least 1.8C of warming.

Kurum and Australia’s climate minister backed a goal for electricity to provide 35% of global energy by 2035, up from about 21%. But Kurum was less definite about renewing a direct commitment to transition away from fossil fuels, despite both countries supporting that wording at the Fiji meeting.

content.headline: Conservatives overstated net-zero cost by nearly £500bn, analysis finds
content.shortHeadline: Tory net-zero cost estimate appears overstated by £479bn
content.standfirst: A Conservative conference document cited £957bn as the cost of reaching net zero, but the underlying Climate Change Committee figures total £478bn. The committee says it does not recognise the larger number; the party has been asked to comment.

image.caption: Kemi Badenoch addresses the Conservative conference in Birmingham.

sources.originalTitle: Tories overstate net zero cost by nearly £500bn in apparent spreadsheet error

segments.body: The Conservatives’ conference policy document says the Climate Change Committee estimated that its route to net zero would cost £957bn. The Guardian reports that the relevant figures in the committee’s 2020 analysis total £478bn, suggesting the document overstated the figure by nearly £500bn.

The apparent error may have come from counting both individual costs and the spreadsheet’s column totals. The committee said it did not recognise the £957bn figure and had offered to explain its advice to Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch. Its more recent analysis puts the expected cost of reaching net zero by 2050 at about £110bn.

The report says the figure may have been copied from a right-wing thinktank report or a Spectator article. The Conservatives and Badenoch’s office were contacted for comment.

content.headline: Royal Navy sailor charged with preparing to pass secrets to Russia
content.shortHeadline: Royal Navy sailor charged in alleged Russia spying case
content.standfirst: Teddy Young, a naval intelligence rating, is accused of retaining sensitive material and preparing to pass protected information to a foreign power. He has not been convicted, and prosecutors have not publicly named the alleged recipient.

image.caption: Teddy Young appears in court at Westminster Magistrates' Court.

sources.originalTitle: Royal Navy sailor charged with spying ‘was working for Russia’

segments.body: Teddy Young, 24, has been charged under the National Security Act after an investigation into alleged attempts to contact Russian authorities through the dark web. Prosecutors say the serving Royal Navy intelligence rating accessed and retained sensitive defence and intelligence material and prepared to pass protected information to a foreign power.

segments.title: Investigation and unanswered questions
segments.body:
Young was first arrested in May 2025 and was suspended from duties, with his security clearance removed, according to the i Paper. He was charged this week and remanded in custody. The CPS has not identified the alleged foreign power in the charges as reported by the outlet.

The report quotes experts who say a junior rank does not necessarily prevent access to sensitive information. They discuss possible motives including money or ideological alignment, but stress that the evidence does not establish why Young is alleged to have acted. Police say the case is not connected to the RAF Fairford investigation.

content.headline: Right to Buy backlog threatens councils' homebuilding plans
content.shortHeadline: Right to Buy sales threaten council homebuilding plans
content.standfirst: Councils expect sales to remain far above government forecasts as they work through a backlog of applications. Analysis by the i Paper suggests more homes may be sold this year and next than the government expects to replace.

image.caption: Council homes are being sold faster than the government expects them to be replaced.

sources.originalTitle: Council housebuilding plan thrown into disarray by Right to Buy surge

segments.body: Councils are still processing a surge of Right to Buy applications made after discounts were reduced in 2024. The i Paper’s analysis of council papers and responses suggests more than 14,000 homes will be sold this year and next, compared with 10,450 replacements forecast by the government.

segments.title: A replacement challenge
segments.body:
The government had expected sales to fall to about 1,650 a year after the initial rush, but councils say applications are continuing to move through the system. Birmingham reported thousands awaiting processing and said it expected 1,500 sales this year, while Leeds forecast 1,150 over two years.

Councils can keep sales income for replacement homes, but Lancaster’s council leader said the sums do not cover the cost of building replacements. The government says its reforms and £39bn investment will mean more social homes are built than sold over the next decade.

content.headline: Data breach exposed 8.8 million CPR numbers through Odense firm
content.shortHeadline: 8.8 million CPR numbers exposed in major data breach
content.standfirst: A company with legal access to Denmark’s civil registration system was compromised, allowing millions of records to be extracted. Documents show the intrusion went undetected for days after it stopped; experts and the company’s owner have raised questions about security and oversight.

image.caption: A graphic illustrates a password used by the company involved in the CPR data breach.

sources.originalTitle: Afsløring: Fynsk virksomhed er centrum for massivt CPR-databrud
Her er den fynske virksomhed cpr-lækket gik igennem
It-ekspert saver sikkerheden over i fynsk virksomhed, der er i centrum for CPR-databrud
Nye detaljer om cpr-skandale – hacker var over alle bjerge

segments.body: A data breach involving about 8.8 million CPR numbers and addresses was carried out through Pays ApS, a small Odense company with legal access to the register. The company confirmed to TV 2 that its access had been misused. It said it was cooperating with authorities and declined an interview.

segments.title: A delay in detection
segments.body:
Documents obtained by TV 2 say the data was extracted between 10 and 20 September, with more than 14 million searches. The breach was detected after an unusually high invoice drew attention; the company’s access was blocked on 2 October. The CPR office said the searches far exceeded the company’s usual pattern.

DR reports that a password used by the company was “123456” and that two-factor verification was not in place. The company did not respond to DR’s request for comment by its deadline.

segments.title: Questions over safeguards
segments.body: IT security expert Peter Kruse and the chair of the Cybersecurity Council criticised the company’s security and questioned whether authorities had adequate safeguards and monitoring for businesses with access to the register. Authorities have not publicly attributed the breach, and no suspect has been identified in the supplied reporting.

perspectives.body: DR reports that Kruse questioned why the system did not automatically halt unusually large volumes of searches, while the Cybersecurity Council chair said the case suggested oversight may have been inadequate.

content.headline: Denmark's budget proposal brings tax changes with uneven gains
content.shortHeadline: Budget proposal gives uneven gains across households
content.standfirst: The government’s proposed tax and benefit changes would give the largest gains to some pensioners and higher earners, while many average-income households may gain little. The package still needs parliamentary approval.

image.caption: Government ministers present the proposed finance bill.

source.credit: Foto: Ida Marie Odgaard / Ritzau Scanpix

sources.originalTitle: Så meget får du med nyt finanslovsudspil
Her er de centrale dele af regeringens udspil til finanslov

segments.body: The government’s finance bill proposal includes tax relief and changes to benefits, but the gains vary across households. A pensioner couple eligible for early retirement could receive a combined 46,000 kroner more after tax each year under the proposal, according to TV 2’s calculations.

segments.title: Who gains and who may lose
segments.body:
The proposal would also give about 150,000 lower-income pensioners an extra 1,600 kroner a month and remove the middle tax for around 600,000 people. TV 2’s financial experts say many households on average incomes may see little change, while young people could lose money if the resident-student grant is reduced. People with large loans could also be affected by a proposed cap on interest deductions.

The bill must win a majority in parliament, and the final measures are subject to negotiations.

content.headline: More Danish children are receiving Wegovy as experts urge caution
content.shortHeadline: Wegovy prescriptions among Danish children rise
content.standfirst: Four hundred and twenty-seven people under 18 filled a Wegovy prescription in the first eight months of the year, already exceeding the total for 2024. An obesity specialist says medication may be appropriate in rare cases, while others urge attention to children’s wider wellbeing.

image.caption: Wegovy use among children and young people in Denmark is increasing.

sources.originalTitle: Flere børn får slankemedicin: Eksperter advarer mod hurtige løsninger

segments.body: New figures show that 427 children and young people under 18 filled prescriptions for Wegovy in the first eight months of the year, compared with 394 in all of 2024. The total puts use among under-18s on course for a new annual record.

segments.title: Careful prescribing urged
segments.body:
Professor Jens Meldgaard Bruun said medication can be necessary for children with conditions related to obesity, but that it is fortunately uncommon. He also noted that Novo Nordisk’s studies suggest treatment may need to continue for life to maintain weight loss.

A leader at a children’s wellbeing centre urged clinicians to consider the reasons behind a child’s weight and to support physical, mental and social wellbeing. Bruun said prescribing and follow-up should be handled by paediatric specialists. Novo says its research is conducted in cooperation with scientific and regulatory authorities.

content.headline: Mette Frederiksen agrees to meet father of Swedish officer killed in Copenhagen
content.shortHeadline: Danish PM to meet father of Swedish officer killed in Copenhagen
content.standfirst: Johan Zedig says a one-year sentence for the man who struck his son is not enough. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen has agreed to meet him and says cases of fatal violence by repeat offenders should be punished more harshly.

image.caption: Johan Zedig speaks about his son, Christian, who died after an assault in Copenhagen.

sources.originalTitle: Far til dræbt betjent vil mødes med Mette Frederiksen
- Jeg ville ønske, de ikke var her, siger Mette F. om bestemte muslimer

segments.body: Johan Zedig, whose son Christian was a Swedish police officer, has invited Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen to Sweden after the man who struck his son was sentenced to one year in prison for assault. Christian died days after being hit during a football-screening event at Copenhagen’s Islands Brygge.

segments.title: The sentence and the law
segments.body:
The defendant admitted the assault but was not convicted of murder, attempted murder or aggravated assault. The prosecutor said the court assessed the typical danger of the punch rather than its fatal consequence. The defendant had previous convictions for serious crimes.

Frederiksen accepted Zedig’s invitation and called the assault senseless. She said cases of simple assault resulting in death, where the offender has a prior conviction for violent crime, should carry much harsher penalties. The report does not say what legislative change, if any, will follow.

content.headline: Russian state TV presents disputed account of encounter with Danish helicopter
content.shortHeadline: Russian TV airs disputed account of Danish helicopter encounter
content.standfirst: Russian state television says a Russian warship fired signal flares to warn a Danish military helicopter away. Denmark’s armed forces describe the flight as routine and say the helicopter stayed about 150 metres from the ship.

sources.originalTitle: Russisk tv viser billeder fra møde med dansk helikopter

segments.body: Russian state broadcaster Russia 1 has aired footage it says shows a 14 September encounter between a Russian warship and a Danish Fennec helicopter south-east of Gedser. The report says the helicopter entered the ship’s security zone and ignored radio calls, prompting the crew to fire signal flares.

segments.title: Conflicting accounts
segments.body:
Denmark’s armed forces say the helicopter was on a routine mission photographing Russian ships in Danish waters. Its pilot said the aircraft was never closer than about 150 metres and described the Russian action as harassing and unsafe.

TV 2 says some footage shown by Russia 1 could be from a different occasion, so it cannot confirm that the images establish how close the helicopter flew. The broadcaster had sought a response from the Danish armed forces.

content.headline: Women warn of adult man speaking with children in Danish Roblox game
content.shortHeadline: Roblox users warn of adult man speaking with children
content.standfirst: Two women say they heard an adult man discussing dating and relationships with girls they believed were under 15 in a Roblox voice-chat game. The platform says voice chat is for verified users aged over 13; a child-safety organisation says age checks are not always effective.

sources.originalTitle: Kvinder rystet over oplevelse i børnespil

segments.body: Two women from Grenaa say they encountered a 34-year-old man speaking with girls they believed were under 15 in the Roblox game Danish Voice. They described an initially ordinary conversation that turned flirtatious and included discussion of dating apps and relationships. Their account has not been independently confirmed in the report.

segments.title: Age checks and safety
segments.body:
The women say they reported the man to Roblox and police. Roblox told TV 2 that voice chat is available only to users over 13 who have been verified by ID or facial scan, but Børns Vilkår says children can pose as older and adults as younger. The organisation advises parents to stay interested in what children do online and to make it easy for them to report uncomfortable experiences.

The women say the man threatened one of them after they challenged him. TV 2 says Roblox declined to comment on the specific case.

content.headline: Eleven people sentenced in serious kidnapping and assault case in Viborg
content.shortHeadline: Eleven sentenced in Viborg kidnapping case
content.standfirst: A court sentenced 11 people to prison for abducting and assaulting a 17-year-old in Viborg. Six have appealed immediately, and four others are still considering whether to challenge their sentences.

image.caption: The 11 defendants were sentenced in the Viborg case.

sources.originalTitle: 11 kidnappere idømt hårde domme i Viborg

segments.body: Eleven people have received prison sentences for the abduction and assault of a 17-year-old in Viborg in April last year. The teenager was attacked at Stationspladsen, forced into a car boot and assaulted again, including in a wooded area near Finderupvej.

Sentences ranged from one year and three months to two years and three months. One defendant will be expelled from Denmark and permanently barred from re-entering, according to the prosecutor. Six of the 11 appealed immediately; four others requested time to consider an appeal.

content.headline: Denmark proposes a 200-kroner fee for cruise passengers
content.shortHeadline: Cruise passengers could face a 200-kroner Danish fee
content.standfirst: The government says a proposed passenger levy would help account for cruise ships’ pollution, noise and congestion. Aarhus port and tourism representatives warn the charge could deter cruise lines and reduce local income.

image.caption: A proposed government charge would apply to cruise passengers arriving at Danish ports.

sources.originalTitle: Krydstogtafgift giver stor kritik: '200 kroner per passager er voldsomt'

segments.body: The government proposes a 200-kroner charge for each cruise passenger arriving at Danish ports, with the levy expected to raise 300 million kroner for the state. The measure is intended to make cruise tourism contribute to the effects of ship traffic, including pollution, noise and congestion.

segments.title: Tourism concerns
segments.body:
Aarhus Port and VisitAarhus criticised the proposal, saying it could make the city and region less attractive to cruise operators and reduce local income. VisitAarhus said 200 kroner per passenger was a substantial charge.

The port says it has invested in shore power, which lets ships switch off diesel engines while docked. The proposal is due to apply from 2028 and has also drawn criticism from Danish business organisations.

content.headline: The Avalanches turn jingles, old tech and memory into a new album and film
content.shortHeadline: The Avalanches make a wild album about memory
content.standfirst: On No Bad Memories, the sample collagists fold vintage jingles, technology sounds and an eclectic cast of collaborators into a restless new record. They also made a surreal short film with Haley Joel Osment.

image.caption: Robbie Chater of the Avalanches, who says the group’s music is built from the memories and humanity in sampled sounds.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Spend time going down rabbit holes’: how the Avalanches created their wildest album yet

segments.body: The Avalanches’ new album, No Bad Memories, turns the sounds of old technology, advertising and children’s TV into a bright, fast-moving collage. The Australian duo say they wanted a joyous record, but its central idea is unsettling: how jingles and electronic sounds can shape and distort what we remember.

segments.title: A record that keeps skipping ahead
segments.body: The album moves between collaborators including John Glacier, Khadija Al Hanafi, Panda Bear and Haruomi Hosono. Chater and Di Blasi also made a 35-minute film, with Haley Joel Osment as an archivist whose own memories become entangled with the material he collects. The band say that clearing samples has become increasingly difficult and costly, even as they return to digging for more.

content.headline: As punk turns 50, musicians around the world explain what it means to them
content.shortHeadline: Punk at 50: musicians on the freedom to question everything
content.standfirst: From a Ukrainian medic-turned-musician to punk scenes in Morocco, South Africa, India and China, artists describe how the genre gives them a language for anger, community and resistance.

image.caption: Musicians from Beton, Twenty One Children, Taqbir and Depustūtes, among the artists reflecting on punk’s reach.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It gave me a superpower – question everything’: ​as punk turns 50, bands from China to Greenland explain how it fires up their lives

segments.body: Punk’s reach is not limited to the places where it first took hold. Musicians from Ukraine, Morocco, South Africa, India, Latvia, China and Greenland describe finding their own versions of the music—and using it to challenge authority, prejudice and the pressure to fit in.

segments.title: A scene built on local ties
segments.body: For Beton’s Andriy Zholob, guitars offered relief during frontline medical service, and his band recorded a Clash cover to raise money for Ukrainian resistance. In Soweto, Twenty One Children’s Abdula Skink connects punk to skating, community work and a DIY skate park. Other musicians describe the risks of performing anonymously or speaking openly about politics.

content.headline: Liz Harris finds a restorative kind of togetherness with Helen
content.shortHeadline: Liz Harris on Helen, collaboration and music-industry scams
content.standfirst: The Grouper musician discusses the contrast between her solitary work and the brighter, collaborative sound of Helen, as well as the royalty fraud that followed a song’s unexpected viral success.

image.caption: Liz Harris, whose work as Grouper is largely solitary and whose band Helen brings a more collaborative side into view.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s rational to fear the music industry’: Grouper’s Liz Harris on virality, streaming scammers and her ‘restorative’ dream-pop trio

segments.body: Liz Harris is used to making music alone as Grouper. In Helen, her dream-pop trio with Jed Bindeman and Scott Simmons, the collaboration brings a different kind of energy. Harris says rehearsing and playing with friends helped lift her spirits while she was dealing with medical difficulties; their second album, Linda’s Head, makes that shared presence audible.

segments.title: When a song goes viral
segments.body: A TikTok revival of Grouper’s 2008 song Poison Tree brought new listeners, but Harris says someone else had fraudulently registered and uploaded it, collecting royalties before she and her label manager were able to shut down the scam and recover what she was owed. She remains wary of streaming platforms’ ability to police impersonation and infringing tracks.

content.headline: Soft Cell’s final album became a farewell to Dave Ball
content.shortHeadline: Marc Almond on Soft Cell’s final album and Dave Ball
content.standfirst: Soft Cell had finished Danceteria when keyboardist Dave Ball died two days later. Marc Almond reflects on a last record shaped by their time in New York and a partnership that lasted nearly five decades.

image.caption: Marc Almond and Dave Ball of Soft Cell, whose album Danceteria became their final record together.

sources.originalTitle: Soft Cell’s Marc Almond: ‘We finished the album – two days later Dave passed away’

segments.body: Soft Cell agreed that their new album was finished in October 2025. Two days later, Marc Almond was told that Dave Ball had died. Danceteria is the duo’s sixth and final album: Almond says he would not make another Soft Cell record without his longtime bandmate.

segments.title: New York, then and now
segments.body: The record looks back to the pair’s early-1980s New York life, with its clubs, experimentation and excess, while also making room for loneliness and the impact of the AIDS crisis. Almond describes the album as a fitting full circle: the two had become closer during its making, and Ball was happy with the finished record.

content.headline: Tom Morello’s first solo rock album turns family history into protest
content.shortHeadline: Tom Morello on protest, family and his first solo rock album
content.standfirst: On Everyone Gets What They Want, the Rage Against the Machine guitarist brings his long-running activism to a first full-length solo rock record. He also reflects on how his mother shaped his politics.

image.caption: Tom Morello, whose new solo album continues his use of music as political activism.

sources.originalTitle: Tom Morello on Rage Against the Machine fans turning against him

segments.body: Tom Morello describes Everyone Gets What They Want as an anti-racist, anti-fascist record for people who have had enough. His first full-length solo rock album puts him at the microphone with the heavy guitar sound associated with Rage Against the Machine, alongside guests including Serj Tankian, Kneecap and his son Roman.

segments.title: A lesson carried forward
segments.body: Morello traces his political outlook to his mother, Mary, who stood up against racism and supported causes from anti-colonial movements to workers’ rights. He recalls her explaining, during a grape boycott when he was six, why their family would go without grapes to support farm workers. He says that belief in ordinary people’s ability to act runs through his songs.

content.headline: Dawn Richard brings New Orleans’ musical blend home on creole culture
content.shortHeadline: Dawn Richard’s New Orleans celebration on creole culture
content.standfirst: The final instalment of Richard’s hometown trilogy trades some of her past experimental edge for a communal, genre-crossing sound. The review finds its warmth compelling, even when the songwriting feels less adventurous.

sources.originalTitle: creole culture

segments.body: On creole culture, Dawn Richard draws on New Orleans through live instrumentation, programmed beats and shifting styles. The album completes a trilogy that began with new breed and continued with Second Line: An Electro Revival, but the review hears a more understated approach to the city’s musical and cultural mix.

segments.title: A lively procession, with limits
segments.body: Songs move between jazz, bounce, reggae, amapiano, gospel and electronic production, often flowing into one another like a DJ set. The review praises the record’s communal pulse and Richard’s versatility, while arguing that a more grounded, less provocative mode leaves some of her eccentric imagination untapped.

content.headline: Cameron Winter’s Carnegie Hall concert becomes a solo live triumph
content.shortHeadline: Cameron Winter turns a Carnegie Hall night into a live album
content.standfirst: The Geese frontman’s solo set reworks songs from Heavy Metal alongside new material, revealing a more open, piano-led performer. The review weighs the music’s intimacy against the mythmaking around the concert.

sources.originalTitle: Live at Carnegie Hall

segments.body: Live at Carnegie Hall captures Cameron Winter’s December 2025 solo performance, including three unreleased songs and material from Heavy Metal. The review hears the songs loosen and breathe in this piano-led setting, with Winter’s shifting pace and touch bringing a new sense of control to music that was more fraught on his studio debut.

segments.title: A concert and its legend
segments.body: The album accompanies a concert film by Paul Thomas Anderson, and the review notes how both preserve the performance while adding to its mythology. It singles out “If You Turn Back Now” and the new songs as highlights, while suggesting Winter’s evasiveness may be a way of protecting himself from the pressure of rising fame.

content.headline: The Beatles’ Rubber Soul reissue brings the album’s contradictions into focus
content.shortHeadline: Rubber Soul, heard again in an expansive new reissue
content.standfirst: A new deluxe edition gathers alternate mixes, outtakes and studio detail around the Beatles’ pivotal 1965 album. The review argues that its changing versions reveal a work shaped by both artistic ambition and commercial circumstance.

sources.originalTitle: Rubber Soul (Super Deluxe)

segments.body: Rubber Soul arrived at a turning point for the Beatles and for pop, with its songs reaching beyond the group’s earlier approach. This expanded edition brings together UK and US versions, mono and stereo mixes, outtakes and a new remix, giving listeners several ways to hear the record’s development.

segments.title: No single definitive version
segments.body: The review finds the box set most persuasive when it exposes what changed between takes and releases, from the album’s track lists to its mixes. Rather than treating Rubber Soul as a fixed monument, it presents a work made under deadline and industry pressure by musicians still experimenting—and suggests listeners’ preferred version may depend on how they first heard it.

content.headline: Peter Greenaway’s unfinished film is caught in a dispute over its final cut
content.shortHeadline: Peter Greenaway’s film is stuck in a post-production dispute
content.standfirst: Three years after filming began in Tuscany, Greenaway’s assisted-dying drama remains unfinished amid a dispute with producers over the cut and the film’s rights. The city of Lucca says it has not received answers about the project’s delay.

image.caption: Peter Greenaway, whose film Tower Stories remains caught in a dispute over its completion and release.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Is death necessary?’: why Peter Greenaway’s assisted dying drama is stuck in post-production hell

segments.body: Peter Greenaway’s film, now called Tower Stories, was conceived as a drama about mortality, featuring Dustin Hoffman as a New York writer returning to his roots in Lucca, Italy. Production was delayed and ran over budget; after an initial assembly was delivered, the director and producers reportedly diverged over which version should be completed and released.

segments.title: A project in limbo
segments.body: The Guardian reports that two unfinished cuts are in circulation and that a dispute over rights remains unresolved. Facing East, the production company, did not respond to requests for comment. Lucca councillor Remo Santini says the city supported the shoot and had seen a preview, but has had no subsequent explanation from the production or director.

content.headline: The Social Reckoning puts Facebook under scrutiny, but critics differ on its aim
content.shortHeadline: The Social Reckoning: a chilling story, or a drama without bite?
content.standfirst: Aaron Sorkin’s sequel draws on reporting about Facebook’s internal practices and whistleblower Frances Haugen. One review finds a frightening portrait of social media’s reach; another argues the film lacks the tension to change anyone’s mind.

image.caption: Jeremy Strong plays Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.

sources.originalTitle: I was terrified watching The Social Reckoning – then went back to scrolling
The new Darth Vader: how tech execs became the film villains of our age
The Social Reckoning review: Aaron Sorkin's drama puts Facebook on trial, but it won't change anyone's minds ★★☆☆☆

segments.body: The Social Reckoning follows Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz and former Facebook employee Frances Haugen as they investigate the company’s internal research and the effects of its platform. Jeremy Strong plays Mark Zuckerberg, while the film’s account of the Facebook Files turns the focus from the company’s origins to its influence and accountability.

segments.title: Two readings of the film
segments.body: The i’s review calls the film a chilling exploration of how social media has reshaped society, while also reflecting on how difficult it can be to stop using Meta’s products. The Guardian’s piece focuses on the change in public perception of Zuckerberg and notes that former employees found parts of Strong’s portrayal recognisable. The BBC’s review, by contrast, judges the drama repetitive and too undramatic to shift viewers’ views.

perspectives.body: The BBC review argues that the film’s lack of danger and dramatic conflict undermines its investigative premise, and that the company’s continued power makes a decisive reckoning feel out of reach.

content.headline: Artificial turns the story of OpenAI into a warning about control and risk
content.shortHeadline: Artificial asks who gets to control AI’s future
content.standfirst: Luca Guadagnino’s drama follows OpenAI’s formation and the conflict between Sam Altman and Ilya Sutskever. Its account of safety, ambition and commercial pressure has gained fresh resonance, though the film’s treatment of Altman is criticised as thin.

sources.originalTitle: AI fears are growing – and unsettling new film Artificial puts them, and the future of humanity, centre stage

segments.body: Artificial traces the formation of OpenAI as a non-profit and its transformation into the company behind ChatGPT. Andrew Garfield plays Altman and Yura Borisov plays Sutskever, whose split over the company’s direction becomes a story about idealism, commercial priorities and who should control powerful AI systems.

segments.title: Off-screen questions
segments.body: The film’s release was complicated when Amazon MGM Studios, which financed it, said it would not distribute the picture; Neon later acquired it. The gathered account notes that Amazon had invested in a partnership with OpenAI, while Altman said he had not spoken with Amazon about the decision. The film’s critique of the industry arrives without any practical, industry-wide safety resolution in sight.

content.headline: Martin McDonagh and his stars discuss guilt, history and Wild Horse Nine
content.shortHeadline: Wild Horse Nine: McDonagh, Malkovich and Rockwell on the film
content.standfirst: John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell play CIA agents stationed on Easter Island in 1973 in Martin McDonagh’s new film. Their conversation ranges from the story’s atmosphere of regret to the actors’ working relationship and McDonagh’s take on political secrecy.

image.caption: Martin McDonagh with actors Sam Rockwell and John Malkovich, who star in Wild Horse Nine.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Old-timey fascism was kept secret. Now you don’t have to hide it’: Martin McDonagh, John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell on Wild Horse Nine

segments.body: Wild Horse Nine follows two CIA agents played by John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell, sent to Rapa Nui after plotting the 1973 coup in Chile. McDonagh says he began writing with “GUILT and REGRET” in mind; the film mixes the director’s familiar odd-couple humour with a more mournful focus on age, death and the past.

segments.title: Two actors, two approaches
segments.body: Rockwell is openly admiring of Malkovich, while Malkovich describes the intensive rehearsals they shared. Their conversation also turns to the film’s treatment of political power and secrecy. McDonagh says covert interventions have become more brazen, but cautions against treating one president as uniquely responsible for the history of US actions abroad.

content.headline: The Lost Children of Tuam recounts a tragedy without easy closure
content.shortHeadline: The Lost Children of Tuam tells a painful story with restraint
content.standfirst: Monica Dolan plays historian Catherine Corless in a drama about the children who died at St Mary’s mother and baby home. The review praises its serious, unsentimental approach to the discoveries and the survivors’ testimony.

image.caption: Monica Dolan as Catherine Corless in The Lost Children of Tuam.

sources.originalTitle: The Lost Children of Tuam review – deeply serious retelling of Ireland’s devastating tragedy

segments.body: The Lost Children of Tuam follows Catherine Corless as she investigates deaths at St Mary’s mother and baby home in County Galway. Her research uncovered death certificates for nearly 800 children but no burial records. The film presents the scale of the tragedy without adding a consoling resolution.

The review praises Monica Dolan’s portrayal of Corless and notes the force of brief appearances by survivors, now middle-aged, who describe lives marked by neglect and abuse. Its account is deliberately restrained, resisting the urge to make a devastating history feel like a neatly resolved drama.

content.headline: Ali G returns with a question about the future of character comedy
content.shortHeadline: Can Ali G revive character comedy for the big screen?
content.standfirst: Sacha Baron Cohen’s return to Ali G raises questions about whether the character’s satire still works in a more polarised Britain. The argument reaches beyond one film to a genre that has struggled to find a place in cinemas.

image.caption: Sacha Baron Cohen as Ali G in Ali G: Who Iz I?

sources.originalTitle: Can Ali G: Who Iz I? save character comedy cinema?

segments.body: Ali G: Who Iz I? brings Sacha Baron Cohen’s character back to the screen, but the film’s relevance is not yet clear. Ali G’s comedy once drew on assumptions about race and popular culture; the piece asks whether those targets still land, or risk reinforcing the caricatures the character was meant to expose.

segments.title: A form in search of an audience
segments.body: The argument places Ali G in a tradition of persona-driven comedy, from Peter Sellers to Austin Powers and Borat. Its future may depend on whether a comic character can still speak to shared social references in a fractured culture. The film’s trailer offers little evidence yet of how Baron Cohen has updated the character’s approach.

content.headline: Animals gives Ben Affleck’s kidnapping thriller little room to breathe
content.shortHeadline: Animals: Ben Affleck’s thriller is short on tension
content.standfirst: A strong cast and a high-stakes kidnapping plot promise a propulsive political thriller, but the review finds Affleck’s new film listless and visually anonymous, with too little to say about Los Angeles.

image.caption: Kerry Washington and Ben Affleck in Animals.

sources.originalTitle: Animals review – Ben Affleck’s dull Netflix thriller is lacking in bark and bite

segments.body: Ben Affleck plays a Los Angeles mayoral candidate whose son is kidnapped on election night. The ransom, a divided family and an enigmatic fixer create the makings of a tense thriller, but the review says much of the action stays inside the family’s wealthy home and circles through arguments without building momentum.

The review also compares the film’s kidnapping plot with Spike Lee’s Highest 2 Lowest, arguing that Animals offers little sense of how its setting changes the material. Gillian Anderson is singled out for committing to a pulpy tone, but the film’s final set-piece and slick visual style leave the critic unconvinced.

content.headline: Sofia Coppola reflects on Lost in Translation and Marie Antoinette
content.shortHeadline: Sofia Coppola on her films, family and the details she notices
content.standfirst: In a conversation with a young aspiring filmmaker, Coppola recalls filming in Tokyo, the teenage perspective behind Marie Antoinette’s soundtrack and the women in her family who shaped how she sees the world.

image.caption: Sofia Coppola at the Venice film festival in 2025.

sources.originalTitle: Sofia Coppola: ‘I’m glad we weren’t kicked out of Tokyo making Lost in Translation’

segments.body: Sofia Coppola says her mother taught her to follow her interests and notice the beauty in ordinary surroundings—an influence she sees in the details of her films. Looking back on Lost in Translation, she recalls filming a few scenes in Tokyo without permission, including moments on a subway and at Shibuya Crossing.

Coppola says she chose contemporary post-punk and new romantic music for Marie Antoinette because the young queen’s age reminded her of her own teenage listening. She also discusses her mother’s behind-the-scenes footage of the film and her continuing pleasure in visiting film sets, where she says she is still impressed by movie-making.

content.headline: Doctor Who faces an uncertain future after its Disney+ partnership ends
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who’s future is uncertain after the Disney+ deal ends
content.standfirst: The BBC has cancelled a planned Christmas special and is seeking a new funding partner, leaving the long-running series without a confirmed next Doctor. Fans and contributors disagree about what went wrong, but want the show back on screen.

image.caption: An illustration showing several of Doctor Who’s incarnations, including Jodie Whittaker and Ncuti Gatwa.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Doctor Who has been off air since its most recent series ended in 2025. The BBC has ended its partnership with Disney+, cancelled a planned Christmas special and put future production out to competitive tender. No replacement Doctor or new partner has been announced, leaving the show’s next steps unclear.

segments.title: A changing institution
segments.body: The feature traces the show’s history of reinvention, from its 2005 revival through successive Doctors and showrunners. Contributors point to uneven scripts and declining viewing figures, while also noting the abuse faced by Jodie Whittaker and Ncuti Gatwa. Lifelong fan Frank Skinner says the series needs to return without losing its core values of kindness and curiosity.

content.headline: The Split Up brings a new British Asian family into the divorce drama
content.shortHeadline: The Split Up moves the family-law drama to Manchester
content.standfirst: The spin-off moves the glossy legal series from London to Manchester, with Ritu Arya leading a British Asian cast. Its writers and producers explain how the show aims to keep the original’s family melodrama while making the new family its own.

image.caption: Ritu Arya leads the cast of The Split Up, the Manchester-set spin-off of The Split.

sources.originalTitle: The Split is back – with a twist

segments.body: The Split Up follows Aria Kishan, played by Ritu Arya, as she prepares to take over her family’s Manchester law firm. Her plans are unsettled by her father’s change of direction, a former partner joining the firm and the death of her mother. Like The Split, the series mixes divorce cases with turmoil at home.

segments.title: A new family, a familiar format
segments.body: Writer Ursula Rani Sarma says she wanted British Asian characters living ordinary, recognisable lives rather than being defined by exceptional circumstances. The series has a predominantly British Asian cast and creative team. Original creator Abi Morgan says its family-centred melodrama remains, while the new writers shape a distinct setting and tone.

content.headline: Romola Garai on Adultery, marital disappointment and filming intimacy
content.shortHeadline: Romola Garai on the questions behind ITV drama Adultery
content.standfirst: Garai plays a married personal trainer drawn into an affair in Danny Brocklehurst’s new drama. She discusses the story’s portrayal of women, intimacy coordination and the family pressures that shape her character.

image.caption: Romola Garai in ITV drama Adultery.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I’ve hit my midlife sexpot era!’ Romola Garai on marital misery, cheating … and sex scenes in cars

segments.body: Adultery centres on Beth, played by Romola Garai, and GP Tom, played by Dominic Cooper, who begin an affair after their teenage children start dating. Garai says the script’s attention to marital disappointment and a woman who has suppressed parts of herself persuaded her to take on a story about infidelity.

segments.title: Making intimate scenes
segments.body: Garai describes how intimacy coordinators now help actors plan sex scenes with clear, technical conversations and a designated person responsible for performers’ comfort. She also hopes the drama shows the consequences of the affair for spouses and children, rather than treating it as consequence-free scandal.

content.headline: Carrie’s new TV adaptation divides critics over what to change
content.shortHeadline: Carrie: two critics disagree over the new adaptation
content.standfirst: The Prime Video series has prompted debate about how it changes Stephen King’s angry, bullied teenager. One account sees an inventive update; another argues it strips away Carrie’s agency and the force of her revenge.

image.caption: Summer H Howell as Carrie in the new Prime Video adaptation.

sources.originalTitle: The Carrie remake made me furious
Why a new TV version of horror classic Carrie is already annoying people

segments.body: Mike Flanagan’s eight-part Carrie moves the story into the present day and makes significant changes to its characters and backstory. In a strongly critical review, The i argues that the new version turns Carrie into a frightened figure with little control, and softens both her mother and the people who torment her.

segments.title: The adaptation debate
segments.body: The BBC’s account also reports fans’ objections to Carrie’s casting and to screen versions that soften the character. It presents a counterpoint from horror scholar Sorcha Ní Fhlainn, who says the new series codes Carrie’s otherness through her home-schooling and clothes, and sees the adaptation as a modern story about bullying and social media. The BBC ultimately praises the series; The i rejects its reinvention.

perspectives.body: The BBC’s account argues that the series works on its own terms as a layered contemporary horror and coming-of-age story, despite changes that have frustrated some book fans.

content.headline: Frasier’s Jane Leeves and David Hyde Pierce revisit Daphne and Niles
content.shortHeadline: Frasier’s Jane Leeves and David Hyde Pierce on Daphne and Niles
content.standfirst: The actors look back on the sitcom’s seven-season slow-burn romance, from a much-loved tango to the audience’s reaction when the pair finally kissed. Their friendship off-screen also endured after the series ended.

image.caption: Daphne and Niles, played by Jane Leeves and David Hyde Pierce in Frasier.

sources.originalTitle: ‘He was devastatingly sexy’: Frasier’s Jane Leeves and David Hyde Pierce on the love between Daphne and Niles

segments.body: Jane Leeves and David Hyde Pierce recall how Daphne and Niles’ relationship developed from a one-sided crush into a long-running will-they-won’t-they story. They discuss the humour and patience in the writing, including the candlelit tango in “Moon Dance” and the moment the characters finally kissed.

segments.title: A partnership beyond the show
segments.body: The actors say the cast became close, and they have remained friends since Frasier ended. Leeves and Hyde Pierce also reflect on how the writers ended the romantic suspense before it wore thin, while Leeves wishes the show had handled her pregnancy differently instead of concealing it with a weight-gain storyline.

content.headline: Bake Off’s audience-choice week gives the tent a welcome shake-up
content.shortHeadline: Bake Off lets viewers set the challenges—and loosens its rules
content.standfirst: The series gave viewers control of the baking tasks for the first time, producing unusual challenges and a sharper tone. The review argues that a little more unpredictability could help refresh the familiar format.

image.caption: Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood judge a week of Bake Off challenges chosen by viewers.

sources.originalTitle: Bake Off is toughening up. Good

segments.body: In Bake Off’s first audience-choice week, viewers set the challenges instead of judges Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood. Bakers made cheesecake with family members, different technical bakes from the same basic cupboard and a wearable showstopper—an experiment that brought more uncertainty into the tent.

The episode was not especially chaotic, but the review welcomes the change and a more openly combative dynamic between Lawson and Hollywood. It also notes a harder edge in the judging, arguing that the programme can keep its warmth while moving beyond the cosy formula that has come to feel dated.

content.headline: Gromit will speak for the first time, in Martin Freeman’s audiobook reading
content.shortHeadline: Martin Freeman gives Gromit an audiobook voice
content.standfirst: The famously silent Wallace & Gromit dog will be heard for the first time in an audiobook of his autobiography. Creator Nick Park says Martin Freeman will read Gromit’s thoughts rather than invent a new speaking voice for him.

image.caption: Gromit, the famously silent dog whose autobiography will be read by Martin Freeman.

sources.originalTitle: Gromit finally gets a voice … and it’s Martin Freeman

segments.body: After 37 years on screen without a spoken word, Gromit will have an audiobook voice: Martin Freeman will read Grand: The Autobiography of Gromit. Animator Nick Park says Freeman will not create a conventional Gromit voice, but will deliver the character’s inner thoughts and wry observations.
The book is due on 22 October. A separate behind-the-scenes experience, Larger Than Life, is also planned for London’s Lightroom, opening on 14 October.

content.headline: Jerry Hall’s unpredictable Traitors game makes her an agent of chaos
content.shortHeadline: Jerry Hall is The Celebrity Traitors’ wild card
content.standfirst: Hall’s impulsive choices and baffling comments have made her an unlikely standout on The Celebrity Traitors. The review argues that her apparent disregard for the game is precisely what makes her compelling.

image.caption: Jerry Hall with fellow contestants on The Celebrity Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: Jerry Hall deserves murder on Celebrity Traitors – but legends live beyond logic

segments.body: Jerry Hall has repeatedly acted against the logic of The Celebrity Traitors, including shouting “haggis” almost immediately during a mission where players could choose to be released at the risk of being murdered. Rather than making her an easy target, the review says her unpredictability has become the show’s source of chaos.

Hall’s unexplained outbursts leave fellow contestants and viewers guessing whether she has a strategy at all. The review suggests that her confidence and extraordinary life have insulated her from the usual pressures of the game—and make it impossible to predict what she will do next.

content.headline: A £350 GTA collector’s box highlights gaming’s growing price barrier
content.shortHeadline: The £350 GTA box points to gaming’s luxury-price problem
content.standfirst: Rockstar’s Grand Theft Auto VI collector’s box does not include the game, which brings the combined cost to £420. The argument is not that merchandise should not exist, but that console gaming increasingly caters to people able to pay more.

image.caption: Grand Theft Auto VI’s Vice City collector’s box, sold separately from the game.

sources.originalTitle: What the £350 Grand Theft Auto ‘collector’s box’ says about the escalating cost of gaming

segments.body: Rockstar’s £350 Grand Theft Auto VI: The Goodtime State – Vice City Collection includes merchandise, but no game or download code. Add the £70 game and the total reaches £420. The writer, a collector who enjoys special editions, argues that the price is striking even by the standards of gaming merchandise.

segments.title: A widening divide
segments.body: The piece connects expensive merchandise to rising console and game costs, suggesting that high-end gaming is increasingly aimed at a smaller group of players with more money to spend. It contrasts that market with the much larger number of people who play free or low-cost games on mobile, and worries that the kinds of games built as expansive worlds are becoming less accessible.

content.headline: Ace Combat 8 delivers thrilling dogfights and a surprisingly moving story
content.shortHeadline: Ace Combat 8 makes arcade flying exhilarating
content.standfirst: The latest entry builds on the series’ accessible, high-speed combat with a more cinematic story and spectacular skies. The review finds its missions thrilling, even if the battle can become confusing and the innovations are incremental.

image.caption: A fighter jet cuts through the skies in Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve.

sources.originalTitle: Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve review – brilliant aerial combat game fulfils the Top Gun fantasy

segments.body: Ace Combat 8 puts players in the role of a pilot whose reputation began as propaganda, then becomes real as the conflict escalates. Its accessible controls, varied missions and beautifully rendered skies make dogfighting feel immediate, with the game leaning into the cinematic rush that has long been part of the series.

segments.title: Combat takes centre stage
segments.body: The review praises the weight of the weapons, the destructible environments and the frantic missions, but says visual clutter can make objectives hard to track. The story also borrows from Top Gun: Maverick, yet its presentation and character work make the reviewer unexpectedly invested. Online multiplayer could not be tested during the review period.

content.headline: Silver Pines turns familiar noir and horror influences into a vivid game world
content.shortHeadline: Silver Pines is a stylish, rain-soaked detective adventure
content.standfirst: This 2D investigation mixes point-and-click puzzles with survival horror, but the review finds its lasting appeal in its carefully built atmosphere, visual design and noir-inspired mythology.

image.caption: A rain-darkened scene from the detective adventure Silver Pines.

sources.originalTitle: Silver Pines review – a stylish, neo-noir detective drama

segments.body: In Silver Pines, a private investigator searches a deserted town for a missing singer-songwriter, collecting clues and opening up new areas as the mystery deepens. The game blends point-and-click exploration with survival-horror combat, where ammunition is limited and weapons can fail.

The review says the familiar mechanics are lifted by detailed environments, rotoscoped animation and lighting that makes each room feel composed. References to Twin Peaks, Blue Velvet and other noir works run through the game, while its puzzles reward patient exploration. Players can lower the difficulty if they would rather focus on the story.

content.headline: Gears of War: E-Day has strong combat but struggles to sustain its ideas
content.shortHeadline: Gears of War: E-Day’s combat excels; the campaign drags
content.standfirst: The prequel recreates the alien invasion that defines the series, and its combat feels better than ever. The review finds the campaign repetitive, however, with too much backtracking and exploration that the game itself punishes.

image.caption: Marcus Fenix in Gears of War: E-Day, which returns to the series’ origin story.

sources.originalTitle: Gears of War: E-Day review – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boring

segments.body: E-Day revisits the beginning of the Gears of War story, showing the invasion that brought its alien enemies to the surface. The review finds the opening hours tense and effective, with ruined streets, tactical cover and familiar chainsaw-equipped rifles establishing the series’ brutal appeal.

The campaign then reuses areas and stretches out its missions, while collectibles and side activities interrupt the drama. The review’s strongest praise is for the combat: movement feels more fluid, environments break apart during firefights and the guns remain satisfyingly weighty. Those strengths, it argues, cannot fully rescue a repetitive campaign.

content.headline: A Resident Evil film recreates the feeling of playing the games
content.shortHeadline: This Resident Evil film captures the games’ sense of peril
content.standfirst: Zach Cregger’s adaptation avoids familiar heroes and instead follows an ordinary character through a world of scarce ammunition, strange encounters and escalating danger. The review argues that this approach understands the games’ structure.

image.caption: Zach Cregger on the set of his Resident Evil film.

sources.originalTitle: How Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil stands out from all other game adaptations

segments.body: The Resident Evil film follows courier Bryan Hodukavich as a virus outbreak traps him in a sequence of dangerous locations. He has little ammunition, finds clues in recordings and emails, and meets characters whose brief exchanges suggest more danger ahead—the review sees these choices as a recreation of playing the games rather than a straightforward adaptation of their plots.

The article argues that omitting familiar leads such as Leon and Claire does not make the film less faithful. Instead, it centres the vulnerability and uncertainty that series creator Shinji Mikami has described as essential to horror. The piece also places it alongside films that explore the mechanics and point of view of video games.

content.headline: GTA VI’s virtual romance prompts questions about real-world boundaries
content.shortHeadline: Does romancing a GTA VI character count as cheating?
content.standfirst: Some social-media users say maintaining the game’s central couple crosses a line, while the discussion also exposes anxieties about attention and connection in real relationships. The article argues that boundaries differ, but the debate is about more than a game mechanic.

image.caption: Lucia and Jason, the couple whose relationship players can develop in Grand Theft Auto VI.

sources.originalTitle: Grand Theft Auto VI: can playing a video game count as cheating on your partner?

segments.body: Grand Theft Auto VI asks players to strengthen the relationship between Lucia and Jason through dates, messages and other interactions. Some social-media users have called that kind of gameplay unfaithful, prompting a wider argument about whether romantic choices involving fictional characters count as cheating.

segments.title: The real concern behind the debate
